No image reference. Text-to-video only. Sora 2, 720p, 16:9.

Concept: a freelance nightlife photographer follows a beautiful club promoter into a hidden motel economy where after-hours parties, pill rumors, debt, recovery clinics, and influencer glamour all blur into one dangerous social circuit. The story should feel fictional and cinematic, but grounded like an observational documentary about real people living inside a scene that is both seductive and sad.

Pacing: savage but readable. 0.4 to 0.8-second trailer cuts, tightening into 0.25-second flash-frames before a silence beat. Music: warped reggaeton/trap pulse, detuned male vocal sample, humid sub-bass, camera-shutter clicks used as percussion, one sudden dead-silent freeze before the final title.

[0:00-0:03 — The Door Opens]
Open on a sharp push-in toward a glowing motel walkway at 3:17 a.m., blue fluorescent light buzzing over wet concrete, palms bending in warm rain. Hard cut to a woman in rhinestone makeup stepping through a club back door, wristband half-torn, phone light flashing against her face. Cut to a documentary-style handheld close-up of a motel room key sliding across a reception counter, then to a crowded room where glittering party clothes, bruised knuckles, fake lashes, and cheap champagne collide in one sweaty frame.

[0:03-0:07 — The Circuit]
Beat drops. Rapid, physically connected cuts follow the same night moving through Miami: a scooter weaving past neon pawn-shop signs, a luxury SUV idling outside a recovery clinic, a dressing-room mirror smeared with lipstick, a dancer adjusting rhinestones under harsh bathroom light, cash counted on a motel comforter, a promoter smiling too hard while watching the door. Keep every shot grounded in human behavior — no glamorized instructions, no procedural detail — just atmosphere, consequences, secrecy, and social pressure.

[0:07-0:10.8 — The Crash]
The camera becomes more unstable. Flash-frames: blue pill-shaped party light, mascara tear, motel carpet, cracked phone, gold chain, sweating hand, police light reflected in sunglasses, empty pool, blackout. A man sits alone on a couch in dim amber light as the party roars silently behind glass. A woman looks directly into the lens, halfway between fame and panic, as if realizing the night has already become evidence.

[0:10.8-0:12 — Title / Silence]
Everything cuts to sudden silence. Hold one haunting still moment: the motel exterior empty at dawn, neon still humming, one heel abandoned on wet concrete. Title slams in clean white letters over blue-black grain: BLUE LIGHT MOTEL. Hard blackout on a camera shutter and sub-bass hit.

No dialogue, no captions, no subtitles, no logos. The feeling is seductive, urgent, unstable, and sad — a rise-and-collapse story happening in real time.

prompt_text:
Create a 12-second cinematic teaser trailer for "THE INFORMER LINE," a fictional Vice-style underground-community thriller about a whisper network of club kids, recovery workers, street racers, and anonymous tipsters mapping the hidden economy of a coastal city. No image reference. Text-to-video only. Sora 2, 720p, 16:9.

Concept: every night, an encrypted voicemail line receives anonymous confessions from people living around the city’s after-hours economy — dealers, drivers, dancers, clinic patients, security guards, rich kids, and runaways. One young woman starts recognizing the same voice across multiple calls and realizes the next confession is describing something that has not happened yet.

Pacing: fast documentary-thriller trailer rhythm. 0.5 to 1-second shots, with controlled acceleration into 0.3-second evidence flashes. Audio: low cassette hiss, chopped voicemail beeps, distant club bass through walls, sirens filtered like memory, one dry silence before the final voice line.

[0:00-0:03 — The Call]
Open on a macro shot of an old answering-machine waveform on a laptop screen in a dark apartment, blue light on tired eyes. Smash cut to a coastal highway at night, headlights streaking through mist. A hand presses PLAY on a voicemail. We hear only texture, not readable words: breath, static, club bass leaking through the phone. Cut to a young woman in a convenience-store parking lot, headphones on, realizing the caller is standing somewhere nearby.

[0:03-0:07 — The City Underneath]
The beat enters as a tense, muted pulse. Handheld cuts move through connected fragments: clinic fluorescent hallway, nightclub bathroom mirror, motorcycle helmet visor reflecting palm trees, motel ice machine, security camera monitor, a beach bonfire after sunrise, a stack of flyers for missing people, a dancer wiping glitter from her eyes, a street racer taping a phone under the dashboard. The world feels real, not glossy fantasy — every person is surviving a system that turns private pain into currency.

[0:07-0:10.7 — Pattern Recognition]
The protagonist pins printed call transcripts on a wall, red thread not as detective cliché but as panic. A voiceprint on screen matches three different identities. Flash-frames: burner phone, hospital bracelet, wet money, parking-lot sodium light, pill bottle silhouette, broken acrylic nail, voicemail timestamp, eyes in a rearview mirror, black ocean. She looks up as the room goes silent; outside her window, a car that appeared in the voicemail rolls slowly past.

[0:10.7-0:12 — The Line Answers Back]
Sudden silence. Close on her face lit by the laptop as a new voicemail begins recording by itself. A whispered processed voice says, almost tenderly: “You were never listening. You were next.” Title slams over a black screen with faint analog scanlines: THE INFORMER LINE. Immediate blackout.

Visual style: grounded contemporary thriller, Vice documentary texture fused with premium streaming cold-open construction. 16:9, 720p, ARRI Alexa-style naturalism, dirty fluorescent blues, sodium yellows, phone-screen cyan, wet asphalt, surveillance grain, handheld urgency, shallow-focus close-ups, fast but legible cuts, no exposition, no subtitles, no extra logos. Keep drug-world details social and atmospheric, never instructional. The hook is paranoia, community, confession, and a city that talks after midnight.
